subject: Huawei raised AI chip prices up to 50%. Memory is why
bodyMarkdown:
Reuters reported yesterday that Huawei has raised the price of its flagship AI accelerator by as much as 50 per cent, and the reason has almost nothing to do with the chip itself. It is the memory sitting next to it, and that same shortage is why the laptop you were planning to buy this fall costs more than it did in the spring.

## What Reuters found

Huawei is now quoting more than 250,000 yuan, roughly 37,000 US dollars, for its Ascend 950DT accelerator card. That is 20 to 50 per cent above the quotes it gave customers about two months ago, depending on contract terms, and the card is not even shipping yet. Reuters puts it in the fourth quarter. Older parts moved too. The Ascend 950PR sold for about 60,000 yuan a card at the start of 2026 and now fetches more than 80,000. The 910C board went from roughly 90,000 yuan to more than 110,000. Cambricon lifted the indicated price of its planned 690 chip by 20 to 30 per cent, and smaller rivals MetaX and Iluvatar CoreX made similar moves. Four companies, same direction, same eight weeks. When that happens, the cause is usually upstream of all of them.

## The bottleneck is memory

**High-bandwidth memory**, or HBM, is DRAM stacked in vertical layers and wired straight into the processor package, so an AI chip can pull training data fast enough to stay busy. Every serious accelerator needs it, and only three companies make it at scale: SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron. Washington tightened export controls on advanced HBM bound for China in December 2024, so Chinese buyers have leaned on grey-market supply that costs them several times what everyone else pays. The legitimate market is tight as well, because memory makers keep steering capacity toward HBM, which pays better than the ordinary DRAM that phones and PCs run on. Beijing wants domestic silicon to replace Nvidia's. The control meant to slow that substitution is mostly making the substitute expensive, which is a slower and stranger kind of success than it sounds.

## What it costs you here

Here is the part that reaches Richmond Hill. Gartner forecast in February that combined DRAM and SSD prices would climb about 130 per cent by the end of 2026, pushing PC prices up 17 per cent and smartphone prices up 13 per cent against 2025 levels, with global PC shipments down 10.4 per cent and phone shipments down 8.4 per cent on the year. Then add the border. Canada's counter-tariffs took effect on Tuesday, September 8, covering 27.6 billion Canadian dollars of US imports at 15, 25 and 50 per cent, with electronics and tools in the 15 per cent band and appliances at 25, per the Department of Finance list. A device can get dearer twice over, once because the memory inside it is scarce and once because of where it crossed the border. The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent on September 2 and flagged upside risks to inflation. This is one of them.

## The takeaway

The US August CPI report lands at 8:30 this morning, and the consensus CNBC published yesterday is 3.4 per cent headline with 2.4 per cent core. The line I will read first is core goods, since that is where memory costs and tariffs would surface earliest if they are surfacing at all. If you need a laptop or a phone before spring, I would buy it now rather than wait for a sale the supply picture does not support. The Bank of Canada decides again on October 28, and a goods-price squeeze like this one makes an argument for cutting harder to build.
